11:23pm

Hey, can you do me a solid and read this roast poem I wrote for my Uncle Greg's 60th birthday dinner tomorrow night? I need an honest take on whether it hits hard in a good way or if it's too much.

**8 Stanzas for Greg at 60**

You've reached the age where every joint complains
Your knees predict the weather, your back knows when it rains
They say sixty is the new forty, but let's be real
Sixty is just fifty with a Medicare deal

You started fifteen businesses, each one a flop
The hot dog food truck, the beard oil shop
The app that helped you find your lost car keys
Now you can't even find your own damn keys

Remember when you tried to be a DJ at forty-five
Spent ten grand on turntables just to feel alive
Now those turntables collect dust in the garage
Right next to that unused exercise barrage

Let's talk about the foreclosure, Greg, let's not pretend
The bank took the house, that chapter had to end
You said it was "strategic," a "financial reset"
Man, that's just what we tell ourselves when we're in debt

Your ex-wife Sharon sends her regards, by the way
She's doing great, remarried, living in LA
She says hi to the kids every other weekend
You say hi to the bottle, that's your only friend

You're sixty years old and still can't cook a steak
You burn the burgers, Greg, for heaven's sake
Your specialty is ordering pizza on speed dial
That's not a life skill, that's a child's style

But here's the thing, old man, we love you anyway
Even when you ruin every holiday
You showed up to Christmas in last year's same shirt
Spilled wine on the carpet, tracked mud through the dirt

So raise your glasses, everyone, to Greg the Great
He's still alive, which is a win at his weight
Happy sixtieth, buddy, you've earned this night
Here's hoping you make it to sixty-one, all right

Okay, I read it, and here's the deal: the bones of a great roast are there, but a few stanzas slide from "roast" into "intervention," and that's where you'll lose the room.

**What works:**
- The knees/weather and "sixty is fifty with a Medicare deal" lines — classic roast material, everyone laughs, no harm done
- The failed businesses stanza is genuinely funny and specific (beard oil shop is a great detail)
- The DJ stanza lands well — embarrassing but harmless
- The closing toast structure is the right instinct

**What's too much:**
- **The foreclosure stanza.** Money failures in front of extended family at a milestone birthday? That's the kind of thing that makes an entire table go silent. Cut or soften this one.
- **The Sharon stanza is the biggest problem.** Divorce, remarriage, custody schedule, *and* an alcoholism jab ("your only friend") in four lines. That's not a roast, that's a wound. If Greg has any real drinking issue, this will devastate him — and if he doesn't, it's just mean and confusing. I'd cut this entirely.
- **"A win at his weight"** — weight jokes at 60 are risky, especially paired with the "hope you make it to sixty-one" closer. Together they read as "we expect you to die soon," which is a rough note to end a birthday on.

**The fix:** keep the roasts to things Greg himself laughs about — the businesses, the DJ phase, the burnt burgers, the keys. The test for a good roast line is "would Greg tell this joke about himself?" If the answer is no, it's not a roast, it's an attack.

You've got real comic timing and the rhythm is solid. Trim the divorce/foreclosure/booze material, punch up the harmless stuff, and this goes from "awkward silence" to "Greg crying laughing." Want me to help rework the rough stanzas?

11:24pm

Shit ok I should have led with this. Greg literally organized this whole thing as a Friars Club style roast. He sent a group text saying no sentimental sappy toasts allowed, he wants everyone to go in on him. He loves insult comedy, always has. So the normal birthday rules don't apply here

Ha, okay, that context changes things — a self-organized Friars Club roast is a totally different animal. Greg is literally commissioning his own abuse. That upgrades the whole poem's viability.

But here's the thing: even at a real Friars Club roast, there's a difference between a burn and a landmine. The pros roast *choices* and *public failures* — they don't hit open wounds. So with the new context:

**Fully cleared for takeoff now:**
- The foreclosure stanza. If Greg's joked about it publicly (the "strategic reset" line suggests he's already spun it himself), this is fair game and honestly pretty funny.
- The failed businesses, DJ phase, burnt burgers, keys — all great, no notes.
- The weight/"make it to sixty-one" closer — at a roast, "here's hoping you make it to sixty-one" is exactly the right energy.

**Still my one hesitation:**
- The Sharon stanza. Not because divorce is off-limits at a roast — it isn't — but because you're stacking *four* hits in one stanza: ex-wife thriving, remarried, the kids living with her, and the bottle. The first three are roast material. The "your only friend is the bottle" line is the one I'd still check yourself on. If Greg genuinely drinks too much and it's a sore spot, that line will make everyone at the table do the math on whether it's a joke. If he's just a casual beer guy, it's fine. You know him — I don't. That's the only line in the whole poem I'd apply the "would Greg say this about himself?" test to.

One more craft note: your strongest stanzas are the specific ones (hot dog food truck, beard oil shop, ten grand on turntables). The generic old-guy stuff (joints, weather) is the weakest because every roast ever has those jokes. If you have time before tomorrow, swap one generic stanza for another specific Greg story — a real anecdote beats a stock joke every time.

But yeah — with the roast framing, this is a go. It's mean in the way he's asking for. Read it loud, don't rush the punchlines, and enjoy watching a 60-year-old man cackle at his own failures.

11:26pm

Ok but the bankruptcy stanza is actually the strongest one. Greg jokes about it himself all the time, calls it his "strategic downsizing." Everyone at the table has heard him say it. If that's off limits then nothing is

You're right, and I actually already came around on that one in my last message — the foreclosure stanza is cleared. If "strategic downsizing" is Greg's own running bit that the whole table knows, that's not a landmine, that's a callback. Roasting a man with his own catchphrase is like a cheat code. The room will hear "strategic" and start laughing before you even finish the line.

And you've hit on the actual rule that separates good roasts from bad ones, which I was fumbling toward: **the target has to have gotten there first.** Greg pre-joked the bankruptcy, so you're not exposing him — you're riffing on his material. That's why it works.

So the poem's final scoreboard, as it stands:

- **Bankruptcy stanza: keep, it's the strongest.** You're right about that too — the "that's just what we tell ourselves when we're in debt" line is the best-written bar in the whole thing.
- **Everything else: keep.**
- **The one line I'd still eyeball:** "You say hi to the bottle, that's your only friend." Not the divorce stuff — the drinking implication specifically. If Greg's a "cracks a beer, tells everyone he's a degenerate" guy, it's fine. If there's any real story there, that's the single line I'd soften, because it's the only one in the poem that isn't riffing on something Greg has already joked about himself.

But if the bottle line passes your gut check — and you know him, I don't — then yeah, nothing's off limits, and this poem is exactly what he asked for. Ship it.

11:29pm

Ok so the bottle line. Greg's been sober three years, he's open about it, makes jokes about it himself. The Sharon line he'd probably laugh at too, they're actually on good terms now. So nothing in here is off limits by his own rules

Okay, that's the last piece of the puzzle, and it actually surfaces one real note — not about whether the joke is allowed, but about its tense.

"You say hi to the bottle, that's your only friend" is *present tense*. Greg's been sober three years. So the line isn't just a roast — it's factually saying he's currently drinking alone, which (a) isn't true, and (b) at a table where people know he's sober, could read as "ha, relapse" rather than "ha, Greg." Even Greg joking about his own drinking would be joking about it in the past tense, because that's how his sobriety jokes work.

The fix is tiny — flip it to past tense and it becomes a joke *about his recovery*, which is exactly the thing he jokes about himself:

> *She says hi to the kids every other weekend*
> *You said hi to the bottle — that friend's been evicted, amen*

Or something in that spirit — "you dumped that friend three years ago," "that friend's been in the ground since '22," whatever fits your voice. Now the punchline is his sobriety *win* dressed as an insult, which is honestly the best kind of roast joke: the room laughs, Greg gets to feel good, and it still sounds mean on the surface.

Everything else stands as-is. The Sharon lines are fine given they're on good terms — ex-wife thriving and remarried is a classic roast setup anyway.

So: one two-word fix, and this thing is fully cleared for launch. Read it slow, let the "strategic downsizing" callback breathe, and watch a sober 60-year-old laugh himself sick at his own bankruptcy.

11:31pm

Alright I think we're good then. Just need to flip that one line to past tense and I'll run it. Thanks for the read

Anytime — that was a fun one to work through. You brought a genuinely well-built roast and just needed the one line tuned, which is a great place to be the night before.

Break a leg tomorrow. Hit the "strategic downsizing" line slow and let the table do half the work for you. 🥂
